edits.definition: Classification is the scientific process of arranging living organisms into groups (taxa) on the basis of shared fundamental characteristics, arranged in a hierarchy of obligate categories — kingdom, phylum/division, class, order, family, genus and species. Its purposes are practical and scientific: it makes the enormous diversity of life (millions of described and undescribed species) studyable, gives every organism a universal scientific name through the rules of nomenclature, provides a system of identification and a place to record new discoveries, and — in its modern phylogenetic form — expresses evolutionary relationships, so that the classification reflects how organisms are related by descent.

Bacteria are unicellular prokaryotic microorganisms: their genetic material — a circular DNA molecule lying naked in the nucleoid region, often with small accessory plasmids — is not enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria are absent. A rigid cell wall of peptidoglycan gives the cell its shape (cocci, bacilli, spirilla) and its response to Gram staining; the plasma membrane may fold inward as mesosomes, and flagella, pili and photosynthetic or chemosynthetic membrane systems equip many species for specialised life. Reproduction is chiefly by binary fission, supplemented for variety by recombination through conjugation, transformation and transduction. Bacteria inhabit nearly every habitat on Earth and drive carbon, nitrogen and sulphur cycles.

Kingdom Plantae comprises eukaryotic, multicellular organisms whose cells possess cellulose walls and whose dominant nutrition is photosynthesis, using chlorophyll contained in plastids. The kingdom spans the algae (in older treatments), bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, united by being autotrophic and by a life cycle showing alternation of generations: a diploid sporophyte generation that produces haploid spores by meiosis alternates with a gametophyte generation that produces gametes by mitosis. Across the groups the evolutionary trend runs from aquatic to terrestrial life, from a dominant gametophyte (bryophytes) to a dominant sporophyte (seed plants), and from naked ovules (gymnosperms) to seeds enclosed within fruits (angiosperms).

Phylum Aschelminthes (also called Nemathelminthes; the roundworms, including Ascaris and Wuchereria) contains bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate animals: their body cavity is a false coelom not lined by mesodermal epithelium. The body is cylindrical, slender and tapered at both ends, covered by a tough cuticle; the alimentary canal is complete with a muscular pharynx and a straight terminal anus; excretion runs through a rennet tube (excretory canal) opening by an excretory pore. Sexes are separate (dioecious), females usually larger than males, fertilisation is internal, and many species are important human and plant parasites, with eggs or larvae resisting unfavourable conditions.

The root is the descending, usually non-green axis of the vascular plant that develops from the radicle of the embryo and grows into the soil. It is distinguished from the stem by the absence of nodes, internodes, buds and true leaves; it bears, instead, unicellular root hairs just behind the growing tip, which vastly increase the absorbing surface. The root is positively geotropic and hydrotropic and negatively phototropic, anchoring the plant, absorbing water and dissolved minerals, and often storing food (carrot, beet) or performing extra functions such as support (prop roots of banyan) and respiration (pneumatophores of mangroves). Primary roots and their branches form the tap root or fibrous root systems.

A fruit is the mature or ripened ovary of a flower, developed after fertilisation: the ovary wall becomes the pericarp (which may be differentiated into epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp) and the ovules become the seeds. In parthenocarpy a fruit sets without fertilisation and is naturally seedless, as in banana; such fruits can also be induced with growth regulators like auxins and gibberellins. Fruits formed from the ovary alone are true fruits; where other floral parts — thalamus, perianth — contribute, the fruit is false, as in apple. Fruits protect the seeds, aid their dispersal by wind, water, animals or explosive mechanisms, and are the economic products of many crops.

The nucleus is the largest, double-membrane-bound organelle of the eukaryotic cell and its controlling centre. The nuclear envelope, pierced by nuclear pores, separates the nucleoplasm from the cytoplasm and regulates exchange of materials; within it the genetic material exists as chromatin — DNA complexed with histones — which condenses into visible chromosomes during division. The nucleolus, a dense rounded body without a membrane, is the site of ribosomal RNA transcription and the assembly of ribosomal subunits. The nucleus directs metabolism, growth and reproduction by regulating gene expression, and carries hereditary information from cell to cell and generation to generation; cells without nuclei (mature RBCs, sieve tubes) lose these capacities.

Enzymes are biological catalysts — almost always proteins, with a few catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) — that enormously accelerate the rates of biochemical reactions without being changed or consumed. Catalysis occurs at the active site, a small pocket formed by the folding of the chain where specific substrate molecules bind; by stabilising the transition state, the enzyme lowers the activation energy, so reactions proceed in seconds that would otherwise take years. Enzymes show high specificity (each acts on a particular substrate or reaction type), work within narrow ranges of temperature and pH, and are regulated by modifiers, inhibitors and feedback so that metabolism responds to the cell's needs.

Interphase is the long growth phase of the cell cycle that occupies more than 95% of its duration, during which the cell is not dividing but is metabolically most active, preparing for division. It has three sub-phases: G1, in which the cell grows, synthesises proteins and organelles, and passes the restriction checkpoint; S (synthetic), in which DNA replication doubles the DNA content (2C to 4C) while chromosomes remain decondensed and invisible; and G2, in which further growth and synthesis of proteins (including tubulin for the spindle) complete preparations. Cells that permanently stop dividing leave the cycle at G1 for the quiescent G0 state.

Mitosis is the equational division of the cell nucleus in which one division of a parent nucleus produces two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number and identical genetic content as the parent. After interphase replication has doubled each chromosome into two sister chromatids, mitosis separates these chromatids — through prophase (condensation and spindle formation), metaphase (chromosomes at the equator), anaphase (centromeres divide, chromatids move to poles) and telophase (nuclear envelopes reform) — followed by cytokinesis. In diploid (2n) somatic cells mitosis thus maintains chromosome number, DNA content and genetic stability, serving growth, tissue repair, replacement and asexual reproduction.

Meiosis I is the reductional division — the first of the two successive divisions of meiosis — in which homologous chromosomes pair and then separate, halving the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n). Its prophase I is long and genetically decisive: chromosomes condense, homologues pair (synapsis) along the synaptonemal complex, and crossing over between non-sister chromatids creates new allele combinations. In metaphase I, paired chromosomes (bivalents) align at the equator with their two centromeres on either side; in anaphase I whole chromosomes — each still of two sister chromatids — move to opposite poles; telophase I yields two haploid nuclei. Sister centromeres do not split, which is why the number, not the chromatid count, is halved.

Meiosis II is the second division of meiosis, and it resembles mitosis in mechanics: the two haploid cells formed by meiosis I divide again without any further DNA replication, so that each of the four final cells receives one chromatid of each original chromosome. Prophase II is brief, metaphase II aligns the chromosomes at the equator with spindle fibres from both poles, anaphase II splits the sister centromeres and pulls the chromatids to opposite poles, and telophase II re-forms four haploid nuclei, followed by cytokinesis. The four haploid cells become gametes (sperm) or spore tetrads; meiosis II thus converts the replicated chromosomes of meiosis I into the unreplicated chromosomes of gametes.

Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate using light energy, occurring in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. As photosynthetic electron transport moves electrons from water through Photosystem II, the electron carriers and Photosystem I, energy released pumps protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen; the resulting proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through the ATP synthase (CF₀-CF₁) complexes as protons flow back into the stroma. When electrons travel the full non-cyclic path from water to NADP⁺, both ATP and NADPH form (non-cyclic photophosphorylation); when electrons cycle back from Photosystem I to the electron chain, only ATP forms (cyclic photophosphorylation), supplementing the ATP the Calvin cycle demands.

Blood is the fluid connective tissue that circulates through the heart and vessels, consisting of the liquid plasma matrix (about 55% of volume) and the formed elements suspended in it (about 45%): erythrocytes (red cells, carrying haemoglobin for oxygen transport), leucocytes (white cells, defending against infection) and platelets (cell fragments that initiate clotting). Plasma is 90-92% water with plasma proteins (albumins, globulins, fibrinogen), nutrients, wastes, gases, hormones and ions. Blood transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients and wastes; distributes hormones and heat; defends through immunity; and maintains homeostasis of pH, water and electrolytes — with clotting sealing breaches while antibody- and cell-mediated defences counter pathogens.

Regulation of kidney function is the hormonal control by which the kidneys adjust urine volume and composition to keep blood volume, osmolarity and pressure within narrow limits. ADH (vasopressin), released by the posterior pituitary when osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in plasma osmolarity, increases water reabsorption in the distal tubule and collecting duct, producing concentrated urine. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) responds to a fall in blood pressure or sodium: juxtaglomerular cells release renin, angiotensin II forms — constricting vessels and stimulating aldosterone — which promotes sodium and water reabsorption and raises blood pressure. ANF (atrial natriuretic factor), released by the atria on rising blood pressure, opposes these mechanisms, causing vasodilation and natriuresis; together they maintain the glomerular filtration rate and homeostasis.

Parthenocarpy is the formation of fruit without fertilisation of the ovules, so that seedless fruits develop. It occurs naturally in banana, pineapple and some varieties of grapes and oranges, and can be induced artificially by treating unpollinated flowers with growth regulators — auxins, gibberellins or cytokinins — a practice of commercial value in producing seedless fruit. Parthenocarpy differs from parthenogenesis (embryo development from an unfertilised egg): here the stimulus of pollination or hormone treatment makes the ovary enlarge and ripen without the ovules forming embryos. Seedlessness improves eating quality and processing value, though such fruits cannot propagate by seed and must be multiplied vegetatively.

The male reproductive system consists of the primary sex organs — a pair of testes, held outside the abdomen in the scrotum, which produce spermatozoa and secrete androgens (chiefly testosterone) from the seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells respectively — together with the accessory ducts that carry and mature the sperm: the rete testis and vasa efferentia leading to the highly coiled epididymis where sperm mature and are stored, the vas deferens rising into the abdomen and joining the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, and the urethra passing through the penis to the exterior. Accessory glands — seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands — add secretions that form the semen.

Spermatogenesis is the process by which the diploid spermatogonia of the seminiferous tubules give rise to haploid, motile spermatozoa. It begins at puberty under the influence of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which releases FSH and LH from the pituitary: FSH acts on Sertoli cells (nourishing the germ cells), LH on Leydig cells (secreting testosterone). Spermatogonia multiply mitotically; some enlarge into primary spermatocytes, which complete meiosis I to form secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II to form four haploid spermatids; spermiogenesis then transforms each spermatid — building the acrosome, condensing the nucleus, forming neck, middle piece and tail — into the mature sperm, released into the tubule lumen.
